Albania.role: independence leader and first prime minister
Albania.rationale: He led the 1912 declaration of independence and the provisional government, making him a legible founder of the modern Albanian state.
Albania.review_note: Present him as one central founder among a broader independence movement, not as its sole author.
Albania.decision_reason: Replaces Migjeni because Qemali is a direct state-founder while remaining distinct from later authoritarian regimes.

Bosnia.role: ban of Bosnia and medieval state-builder
Bosnia.rationale: His reign strengthened early Bosnian statehood, trade, and diplomacy; the Charter of Ban Kulin is a durable civic symbol of Bosnian political history.
Bosnia.review_note: A medieval territorial figure who predates modern Bosniak, Croat, and Serb national identities; never use him as a demographic stand-in.
Bosnia.decision_reason: Replaces Mak Dizdar with a shared territorial ruler whose legacy can speak to multiethnic Bosnia without selecting a modern wartime leader.

Bulgaria.role: liberation organizer and republican civic leader
Bulgaria.rationale: He built an internal movement for Bulgarian liberation and articulated a republican ideal of equal citizenship, making him the country's clearest civic-independence avatar.
Bulgaria.review_note: His revolutionary struggle included political violence; emphasize organizing, sacrifice, and civic equality rather than combat spectacle.
Bulgaria.decision_reason: Replaces Ivan Vazov because Levski directly led the independence movement and is broadly recognized as a national civic hero.

Croatia.rationale: He organized rural citizens into a major democratic movement and pressed for Croatian political rights through mass politics and parliamentary action.
Croatia.review_note: His interwar politics belong to a contested Yugoslav setting; avoid martyr iconography and present his democratic organizing rather than later nationalist appropriation.
Croatia.decision_reason: Replaces Ivana Brlić-Mažuranić because Radić provides a recognizable civic and political leadership story.

Macedonia.rationale: He guided Macedonia to independence without the war that engulfed other Yugoslav republics and helped establish its parliamentary constitutional order.
Macedonia.review_note: Retain the roster's historical display name while acknowledging today's North Macedonia; contextualize his earlier career in socialist Yugoslavia.
Macedonia.decision_reason: Replaces Toše Proeski because Gligorov is the clearest modern state-founder and a rare regional example of negotiated, peaceful separation.

Montenegro.rationale: He centralized permanent institutions, introduced taxation, opened a printing press and school, and joined political leadership with an enduring literary legacy.
Montenegro.review_note: The violent religious-national imagery and contested interpretations of The Mountain Wreath require context; emphasize institutions and education, not ethno-religious conflict.
Montenegro.decision_reason: Replaces Petar Lubarda because Njegoš directly shaped Montenegrin state institutions and remains its best-known historical ruler-writer.

Serbia.role: independence uprising leader and state founder
Serbia.rationale: As leader of the First Serbian Uprising, he helped establish the institutions and political precedent from which modern Serbian autonomy and statehood developed.
Serbia.review_note: Sources dispute whether he was born in 1762 or 1768. His uprising involved wartime violence; frame him as a historically significant independence leader, not a spotless moral model.
Serbia.decision_reason: Replaces Nadežda Petrović because Karađorđe is a foundational political leader, while the uncertainty and violence are explicitly disclosed.

Slovenia.rationale: As the first speaker of Slovenia's freely elected parliament and a principal author of its constitution, he helped turn democratic independence into durable institutions.
Slovenia.review_note: His selection represents constitutional and parliamentary leadership rather than any current Slovenian party.
Slovenia.decision_reason: Replaces Jože Plečnik because Bučar directly built the democratic framework of the independent Slovenian state.

Yugoslavia.rationale: As Yugoslavia's last prime minister, he pursued economic stabilization, pluralist reform, and a peaceful democratic federation as nationalism pulled the country apart.
Yugoslavia.review_note: He was a former communist official and his reform program ultimately failed; use him as the avatar of non-authoritarian federal reform, not nostalgia for one-party rule.
Yugoslavia.decision_reason: Replaces Ivo Andrić because Marković offers an actual all-Yugoslav reform-leadership story without selecting an authoritarian ruler.

Armenia.role: independence leader and First Republic founder
Armenia.rationale: He organized defense, relief, and civil administration during national catastrophe and became a principal founder and interior minister of the First Republic of Armenia.
Armenia.review_note: His revolutionary and wartime record, including the defense of Van, needs sober context; emphasize relief, administration, and state-building rather than combat.
Armenia.decision_reason: Replaces Aram Khachaturian because Manukian is directly tied to modern Armenian statehood and emergency civic leadership.

Azerbaijan.role: independence leader and National Council chairman
Azerbaijan.rationale: He chaired the Azerbaijani National Council and became a defining advocate of the secular parliamentary republic founded in 1918.
Azerbaijan.review_note: He was one of several founders of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic; avoid presenting him as its sole creator or as an endorsement of a present-day party.
Azerbaijan.decision_reason: Replaces Uzeyir Hajibeyov because Rasulzade supplies a clear democratic state-founding narrative.

Belarus.role: poet, civic voice, and cultural nation-builder
Belarus.rationale: His writing helped establish modern Belarusian literary language and voiced the dignity and self-definition of a people caught between empires and states.
Belarus.review_note: He worked under intense Soviet pressure and his fatal fall remains disputed; distinguish his civic-cultural legacy from later state appropriation.
Belarus.decision_reason: Keeps the current figure because no deceased political founder is as broadly inclusive, while Kupala clearly qualifies as a civic and cultural nation-builder.

Georgia.rationale: He led the Democratic Republic of Georgia's government and helped build a pluralist modern state before the 1921 Soviet invasion forced it into exile.
Georgia.review_note: His Menshevik party identity and long government-in-exile role need context; the avatar should stand for the democratic republic, not modern partisanship.
Georgia.decision_reason: Replaces Niko Pirosmani because Zhordania provides direct democratic state-building leadership.

Kazakhstan.rationale: He organized the Alash movement and government around national autonomy, representative politics, education, and protection of Kazakh land and culture.
Kazakhstan.review_note: His name also appears as Alikhan Bökeikhan; note his execution during Stalin's purges and avoid converting his legacy into present-day partisan branding.
Kazakhstan.decision_reason: Replaces Abai Qunanbaiuly because Bukeikhanov translates cultural awakening into direct modern political and institutional leadership.

Kyrgyzstan.role: stateswoman and ruler of the Alai Kyrgyz
Kyrgyzstan.rationale: She exercised recognized political authority in the Alai and chose negotiation under extreme pressure to protect her people during Russian annexation.
Kyrgyzstan.review_note: Her accommodation of imperial rule occurred under duress; do not romanticize Russian conquest or reduce her to the nickname 'Queen of the Alai.'
Kyrgyzstan.decision_reason: Replaces Chingiz Aitmatov because Kurmanjan Datka offers nationally resonant political leadership while preserving a humane survival story.

Russia.rationale: He turned from weapons science to a sustained defense of conscience, civil liberties, disarmament, and democratic reform, becoming a globally recognized Russian civic leader.
Russia.review_note: His major role in developing the Soviet hydrogen bomb is essential context; depict the moral turn toward human rights rather than erasing the earlier work.
Russia.decision_reason: Replaces Leo Tolstoy because Sakharov offers modern, concrete civic-reform leadership distinct from the Soviet head-of-state avatar.

Tajikistan.role: statesman and co-founder of Tajik statehood
Tajikistan.rationale: He was instrumental in establishing Tajik political institutions and advancing the republic's status before being executed in Stalin's Great Purge.
Tajikistan.review_note: His work unfolded inside the Soviet party-state and later official hero-making; present both that context and his execution on false charges.
Tajikistan.decision_reason: Replaces Mirzo Tursunzoda because Shotemur is directly connected to institutional Tajik state formation.

Turkmenistan.rationale: His use of Turkmen language and vision of shared Turkmen identity made him a civic-cultural founder long before a modern Turkmen state existed.
Turkmenistan.review_note: Dates and transliterations vary, and modern governments have appropriated his image; keep the presentation centered on language and shared cultural identity.
Turkmenistan.decision_reason: Keeps the current figure because he is more inclusive than Turkmenistan's deceased authoritarian rulers and already qualifies as a cultural nation-builder.

Ukraine.role: historian, statesman, and head of the Central Rada
Ukraine.rationale: He connected scholarship about Ukraine's distinct history with leadership of the Central Rada during the democratic state-building of 1917–1918.
Ukraine.review_note: He is often informally called president, but 'head of the Central Rada' is the safer formal description; his socialist politics should not be mapped onto current parties.
Ukraine.decision_reason: Replaces Lesya Ukrainka because Hrushevsky combined cultural nation-building with direct democratic institutional leadership.

USSR.role: Soviet reform leader and final head of state
USSR.rationale: He introduced glasnost and perestroika, widened political freedom, negotiated major arms reductions, and allowed the Cold War order in Europe to end without a general war.
USSR.review_note: His legacy is sharply contested across successor states and includes late-Soviet crises; the selection represents reform and de-escalation, not endorsement of all Soviet policy.
USSR.decision_reason: Replaces Yuri Gagarin because Gorbachev is a genuine Soviet leader whose defining legacy is reform rather than totalitarian consolidation.

Uzbekistan.rationale: As both a Timurid statesman and the defining champion of Chagatai literary culture, he joins public service with the linguistic foundation of modern Uzbek identity.
Uzbekistan.review_note: He was born and served in Herat and belongs to a wider Central Asian heritage; do not imply citizenship in the modern Uzbek state.
Uzbekistan.decision_reason: Keeps the current figure because Nava'i already satisfies the leadership brief as both a statesman and a cultural nation-builder.

Austria.rationale: Her administrative, educational, and fiscal reforms helped shape the institutions from which the modern Austrian state developed.
Austria.review_note: She ruled a multinational hereditary monarchy rather than modern democratic Austria; the avatar should acknowledge imperial warfare and absolute rule.
Austria.decision_reason: Replaces Gustav Klimt because she provides an unusually recognizable female state-builder and a stronger leadership fit.

Belgium.role: prime minister, diplomat, and European integration pioneer
Belgium.rationale: He led Belgium, served as the first president of the United Nations General Assembly, and helped build Benelux, NATO, and the institutions that became the European Union.
Belgium.review_note: Spaak was a Francophone Belgian and should not be presented as a demographic stand-in for Belgium's Dutch-, French-, and German-speaking communities.
Belgium.decision_reason: Replaces René Magritte and avoids colonial monarchs—especially Leopold II—because Spaak offers significant democratic and international leadership without celebrating colonial atrocities.

Cyprus.role: independence leader, archbishop, and first president
Cyprus.rationale: As the republic's first president, he is the most recognizable individual associated with independent Cypriot statehood.
Cyprus.review_note: His legacy is contested, particularly between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot historical narratives; never imply that he represents every Cypriot community.
Cyprus.decision_reason: Replaces Michael Cacoyannis because Makarios has the clearest founding-state connection, but the bicommunal sensitivity requires explicit contextual review.

Denmark.rationale: She exercised effective rule over Denmark, Norway, and Sweden and created the political framework of the Kalmar Union.
Denmark.review_note: Her dynastic Nordic realm should not be portrayed as a modern Danish nation-state or as uncomplicated national expansion.
Denmark.decision_reason: Replaces Hans Christian Andersen because she was a genuine and highly capable ruler, gives the roster valuable gender balance, and is more directly connected to leadership.

Finland.rationale: He helped design Finland's republican constitution and established democratic presidential government after independence and civil war.
Finland.review_note: His reconciliation work should be presented as part of a broader national recovery rather than a single-person achievement.
Finland.decision_reason: Replaces Jean Sibelius and was chosen over Mannerheim to center constitutional democracy while avoiding the latter's more complicated civil-war and wartime associations.

France.role: Free French leader and founding president of the Fifth Republic
France.rationale: He embodied French resistance during the Second World War and later rebuilt the country's governing framework through the Fifth Republic.
France.review_note: Flavor text should acknowledge the controversies surrounding executive power, empire, and the Algerian War.
France.decision_reason: Replaces Victor Hugo because de Gaulle is France's clearest modern state-reconstruction leader and a highly recognizable visual avatar.

Germany.role: first federal chancellor and democratic reconstruction leader
Germany.rationale: He helped establish West Germany's democratic institutions, international rehabilitation, and reconciliation with France and Israel after Nazism.
Germany.review_note: He governed West Germany; the unified Germany NationId also contains East German experiences that his avatar cannot represent by itself.
Germany.decision_reason: Replaces Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and was chosen over military or nationalist founders to make post-Nazi democratic reconstruction the central leadership story.

Greece.rationale: He modernized Greek institutions, advanced constitutional government, and later pursued regional reconciliation after decades of conflict.
Greece.review_note: His territorial nationalism, revolutionary activity, the National Schism, compulsory population exchange, and connection to Greco-Turkish conflict require honest context.
Greece.decision_reason: Replaces Aristotle to supply a modern governing and reform legacy rather than using an ancient philosopher as the avatar of the modern state.

Iceland.rationale: His sustained constitutional and scholarly campaign became the central civic foundation of Iceland's movement toward self-government.
Iceland.review_note: He died before full sovereignty and independence, which emerged through a longer collective political process.
Iceland.decision_reason: Replaces Halldór Laxness because Sigurðsson is Iceland's clearest nonviolent nation-building leader.

Ireland.rationale: He demonstrated the power of mass constitutional politics through Catholic emancipation while also becoming a prominent opponent of slavery.
Ireland.review_note: His Catholic-national movement does not encompass Protestant, unionist, or every later Irish political tradition.
Ireland.decision_reason: Replaces W. B. Yeats and was chosen over armed revolutionaries and later partisan leaders because his nonviolent organizing and abolitionism make him a broadly defensible civic avatar.

Italy.role: republican general and Italian unification leader
Italy.rationale: His volunteer campaigns supplied the popular revolutionary force that helped transform several states into a unified Italy.
Italy.review_note: The violence of unification and its contested legacy in southern Italy should not be reduced to a triumphalist adventure.
Italy.decision_reason: Replaces Leonardo da Vinci because Garibaldi is the most immediately recognizable popular leader directly connected to building the Italian state.

Luxembourg.role: grand duchess and wartime national-unity leader
Luxembourg.rationale: Her broadcasts and government-in-exile presence made her a durable symbol of Luxembourg's independence, liberation, and postwar stability.
Luxembourg.review_note: Her constitutional and symbolic role should be shown alongside the work of the elected government, resistance, and wider population.
Luxembourg.decision_reason: Replaces Edward Steichen because Charlotte is Luxembourg's strongest recognizable national-unity figure and is much more closely tied to state leadership.

Malta.rationale: He led the negotiations, constitutional preparation, and government that brought Malta to independence in 1964.
Malta.review_note: Dom Mintoff and the later creation of the republic form an equally important competing political tradition; the card should not erase that partisan balance.
Malta.decision_reason: Replaces Dun Karm Psaila because Borg Olivier has the most direct connection to Malta's constitutional independence and state formation.

Netherlands.role: leader of the Dutch Revolt and founding prince
Netherlands.rationale: His leadership against Habsburg rule placed him at the center of the political struggle from which the independent Netherlands emerged.
Netherlands.review_note: The Dutch Revolt was a violent early-modern religious and political conflict, not the birth of a fully modern liberal democracy.
Netherlands.decision_reason: Replaces Rembrandt because William is the canonical founding-state leader and gives the Netherlands a more direct political identity.

Norway.role: constitutional monarch and wartime resistance symbol
Norway.rationale: After accepting the crown through a plebiscite, he respected parliamentary government and later became the foremost royal symbol of resistance to Nazi occupation.
Norway.review_note: Norwegian resistance and liberation were collective achievements involving parliament, government, armed forces, civilians, and allies—not the king alone.
Norway.decision_reason: Replaces Fridtjof Nansen because Haakon's combination of constitutional restraint and wartime resolve makes him a strong, recognizable leadership avatar.

Portugal.role: democracy leader, prime minister, and president
Portugal.rationale: After opposing dictatorship, he helped consolidate pluralist democracy and anchored Portugal's transition toward European integration.
Portugal.review_note: He was a Socialist partisan, and the Carnation Revolution and democratic transition were collective achievements involving many political currents.
Portugal.decision_reason: Replaces Fernando Pessoa and was chosen over imperial-era monarchs, colonial explorers, and dictatorship figures to center Portugal's democratic transformation.

Spain.rationale: He used negotiation and political legalization to help transform Franco's dictatorship into a multiparty constitutional democracy.
Spain.review_note: His earlier career inside Francoist institutions must not be erased, even though he later played a decisive democratic role.
Spain.decision_reason: Replaces Miguel de Cervantes and was chosen over monarchs and military leaders because consensus-based democratic transition is the strongest constructive modern leadership story.

Sweden.rationale: His independent international civil service and peace diplomacy made him one of Sweden's most consequential civic leaders on the world stage.
Sweden.review_note: He led the United Nations rather than Sweden, and his Congo record remains an active subject of historical scrutiny.
Sweden.decision_reason: Replaces Astrid Lindgren because a civic international leader avoids a more divisive royal or partisan choice while retaining a powerful leadership legacy.

Switzerland.role: humanitarian organizer and Red Cross co-founder
Switzerland.rationale: His response to battlefield suffering inspired the Red Cross movement and helped establish international humanitarian law.
Switzerland.review_note: He was a Geneva-born Francophone civic figure, not a proxy for Switzerland's multilingual population or collegial political system.
Switzerland.decision_reason: Keeps the current figure because Switzerland's decentralized leadership tradition makes Dunant's globally influential civic leadership more fitting than elevating one partisan politician.

UK.role: prime minister and postwar reconstruction leader
UK.rationale: His government built the National Health Service and modern welfare state while guiding Britain through postwar reconstruction and major decolonization.
UK.review_note: The avatar must acknowledge contested imperial withdrawal, the partition of India and Palestine, nuclear-weapons policy, and the United Kingdom's multinational character.
UK.decision_reason: Replaces Ada Lovelace and was chosen over Churchill to foreground democratic reconstruction and social institution-building without making imperial and racial controversy the country's default identity.

Czechoslovakia.rationale: He turned civic resistance to communist rule into democratic leadership as Czechoslovakia's final president after the Velvet Revolution.
Czechoslovakia.review_note: Havel was Czech rather than Slovak and opposed dissolving the federation; never present him as embodying both national identities without qualification.
Czechoslovakia.decision_reason: Replaces Karel Čapek because Havel uniquely bridges peaceful dissidence, the 1989 transition, and leadership of the actual Czechoslovak state.

Estonia.rationale: He helped explain Estonia's historical continuity abroad and gave its restored democratic republic a confident diplomatic identity.
Estonia.review_note: He became president in 1992 and represents restoration of the republic, not its original 1918 founding or every strand of the independence movement.
Estonia.decision_reason: Replaces Lydia Koidula and was chosen over interwar leaders with authoritarian associations because Meri offers a clear democratic-restoration legacy.

Hungary.rationale: He converted reform ideas into institutions and infrastructure, supporting the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, transport links, commerce, and civic modernization.
Hungary.review_note: He was an aristocrat operating within the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary, not a modern elected national leader.
Hungary.decision_reason: Replaces Béla Bartók because Széchenyi's practical reform and institution-building provide a constructive alternative to military, authoritarian, or aggressively nationalist figures.

Latvia.rationale: He organized diplomacy for Latvian independence and established the restrained, democratic character of the new republic's presidency.
Latvia.review_note: The state was created through collective political, military, and diplomatic work; Čakste should not be treated as its sole founder.
Latvia.decision_reason: Replaces Rainis; the first democratic president is a safer and more institutionally fitting choice than authoritarian later leader Kārlis Ulmanis.

Lithuania.role: independence activist and nation-building civic leader
Lithuania.rationale: He nurtured Lithuanian civic and cultural institutions, chaired the 1917 Lithuanian Conference, and signed the 1918 Act of Independence first.
Lithuania.review_note: He was a civic organizer and signatory rather than the executive ruler of the new state.
Lithuania.decision_reason: Replaces Mikalojus Konstantinas Čiurlionis and was chosen over authoritarian presidents and medieval conquerors because his contribution joins national revival with civilian independence-building.

Moldova.rationale: His long reign strengthened medieval Moldavia's institutions, defenses, diplomacy, architecture, and written culture.
Moldova.review_note: He belongs to shared Moldovan and Romanian heritage, ruled through medieval warfare, and has accumulated nationalist and religious mythology; his birth year is uncertain.
Moldova.decision_reason: Replaces Maria Bieșu because Stephen is the most recognizable leader rooted directly in historical Moldavia, but shared-heritage and medieval-context caveats make specialist review important.

Poland.role: republican independence leader and military engineer
Poland.rationale: He led resistance to Poland's partitions while promoting republican liberty and challenging serfdom, after also serving the American Revolution.
Poland.review_note: His identity and career are shared with Lithuanian, Belarusian, Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and American history.
Poland.decision_reason: Replaces Frédéric Chopin and was chosen over Józef Piłsudski to retain an iconic independence leader while avoiding the latter's authoritarian rule.

Romania.rationale: His double election united Moldavia and Wallachia, while his agrarian, educational, legal, and administrative reforms laid foundations for modern Romania.
Romania.review_note: His later rule included an authoritarian turn and ended in forced abdication; modernization should not be presented as an unqualified personal triumph.
Romania.decision_reason: Replaces George Enescu because Cuza is the most direct unifier and institutional founder of modern Romania without relying on later extremist leaders.
